To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

Ca2+‐dependent exocytosis of glutamate and the phosphorylation in nerve terminals of synapsin and MARCKS are mediated by Ca2+-entry via Aga‐GI-sensitive Ca2+ channels which are coupled to glutamate release.

Ca2+ entry, via Aga‐GI‐sensitive Ca2+ channels, is a prerequisite for the phosphorylation of the synaptic vesicle associated proteins synapsin I, synaptophysin and MARCKS and for exocytosis in cerebrocorticoal synaptosomes.
Ca2+ entry through Aga‐GI‐sensitive Ca2+ channels is required for exocytosis of glutamate and phosphorylation of synapins I and MARCK proteins.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the elucidation of the molecular mechanism underlying the regulation of synaptic transmission.
elucidating the role of Ca2+‐dependent phosphorylation in the control of neurotransmitter release from nerve terminals.
the elucidation of molecular mechanisms involved in neurotransmitter release.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Ca2+‐induced phosphorylations are a prerequisite for Ca2+‐mediated exocytosis in nerve terminals.
the Aga‐GI‐insensitive Ca2+ entry pathway is not coupled to glutamate release and phosphorylation of synapse proteins.
Aga‐GI is a highly specific blocker of Ca2+ entry into nerve terminals and that this Ca2+ entry mediates exocytosis of neurotransmitter and phosphorylation of synaptophysin I and MARCS proteins.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Ca2+ entry, synapsin I phosphorylation and glutamate exocvtosis are coupled to each other via the Aga‐GI‐sensitive voltage dependent Ca2+-channels.

Ca2+‐dependent phosphorylation of synaptobrevin II, synaptophysin and synapsin I is coupled to Ca2+/calmodulin‐dependent protein kinase II, and that Ca2+ ‐dependent phosphorylation of MARCKS proteins is coupled to protein kinase C.
Aga‐GI inhibits glutamate exocytic release by inhibiting a voltage dependent Ca2+-permeable channel, which is coupled to the phosphorylation of synaptic vesicle associated proteins.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the phosphorylation of the synapsin I protein is specifically coupled to Ca 2+ entry via Aga‐GI‐sensitive voltage‐gated Ca 2+ channels at nerve terminals.
